title: Read the overlaps
setup_tex: Take three views of a point in $\mathbb R^3$: its $xy$, $yz$, and $xz$ coordinates. The picture follows $P=(2,1,3)$ into the three coordinate planes.
reading_tex: Each pairwise view omits one coordinate. The three displayed pairs agree wherever a coordinate is shared, so they describe the same point. Replacing $(2,3)$ in the $xz$ view by $(4,3)$ creates a conflict: the $xy$ view still requires $x=2$.
experiment_tex: Keep only the $xy$ appearance $(2,1)$. The compatible points are the whole line $(2,1,z)$. Restoring the $yz$ appearance $(1,3)$ selects $z=3$.

title: Slice the extension fiber
setup_tex: Use integer variables with $k=2m$ and an independent coordinate $z$. Prescribe $k$, then look for lattice points in that slice. Only three values of $z$ are displayed.
reading_tex: The slice $k=2$ contains $(2,1,z)$ for every integer $z$. The slice $k=3$ misses the lattice because the required $m=3/2$ is not an integer. The free vertical coordinate changes the number of answers, while the parity condition still determines whether any answer exists.
experiment_tex: Prescribe $z=0$ as well as $k=2$. The circled point $(2,1,0)$ is now the unique answer. Prescribing $z=0$ cannot rescue the blocked slice $k=3$.

title: Retain the comparison that matters
setup_tex: Duplicate a view and use the coefficient group $C_2$. A gauge $(a_0,a_1)$ changes the transition label by $r^{\prime}=a_0+r-a_1$. Compare $r=1$ with $r^{\prime}=0$. All arithmetic in this example is modulo two.
reading_tex: Two gauges relate the unmarked labels. The boundary marks $\phi=0$ and $\psi=1$ impose $\psi+a_0=\phi$, leaving one compatible comparison. Freezing both representative gauges instead allows only $(0,0)$, which cannot change the transition label. The three panels retain different data.
experiment_tex: Change the target mark to $\psi=0$ while keeping $\phi=0$. The boundary equation then selects $(0,1)$: a comparison still exists, but the chosen mark determines which one.

title: Find the missing equation
setup_tex: On three ordered views, assign bit labels $c_{01}=0$, $c_{12}=0$, and $c_{02}=1$. Each two-view patch contains its own arrow, but no patch contains the full composition.
reading_tex: The left triangle exposes the unchecked equation: the direct label is one, while the two-step label is zero. On the right, use four ordered views and all four three-view patches. Labels $c_{ij}=a_i+a_j$ from $a=(0,1,0,1)$ satisfy every face equation.
experiment_tex: Replace the left direct label by zero. Its composition equation then holds. This repairs that example; the pair-patch cover still provides no general guarantee that composition was checked locally.

title: Reverse the order
setup_tex: Label the coordinate swap $X$ by $(1,0)$ and the second-coordinate reflection $Z$ by $(0,1)$. Start at $v=(1,2)$ and follow both orders. Matrix products act from right to left.
reading_tex: Both routes use the same two-bit labels, whose sum is $(1,1)$. Their final vectors are negatives because $ZX=-XZ$. In this model the phase $c(x,y)=x_2y_1$ records that sign. The composition law remains associative; reversing these two factors is the operation that changes the result.
experiment_tex: Attach a sign bit to the two-bit label. These two routes then end at different sign bits over the same label $(1,1)$, retaining the distinction that the four labels alone omit.

title: Keep the discarded detail
setup_tex: Compare constant values $g_n=1$ with alternating values $f_n=(-1)^n$ on identity scalar towers. Keep only even levels. The plot displays levels zero through four and their four adjacent defects.
reading_tex: The sampled values agree, and each pair of alternating defects sums to zero. The coarse residual therefore cannot distinguish the candidates. The detail does: with $J(c_0,c_1)=(0,c_0,0,c_1)$, the zero coarse residual lifts to zero, leaving the entire alternating residual in $Hr=r-JCr$.
experiment_tex: Restore the omitted odd values. The alternating candidate has defects $-2,2,-2,2$ while the constant candidate has zero defects. Exact coherent points are unaffected by this example of cancellation in raw candidates.

title: Follow the remainder
setup_tex: For the shift cascade, $Q_Nx$ sets the first $N$ coordinates to zero and leaves the tail in its original positions. Compare the constant sequence with $x_i=2^{-i}$.
reading_tex: The recovered region grows in both panels: every fixed coordinate eventually becomes zero in the remainder. The constant tail keeps height one, so its uniform error never decreases. The geometric tail starts at $2^{-N}$ and then decreases further, giving exactly the norm printed beneath the right panel.
experiment_tex: At depth $N=3$, coordinates zero, one, and two are recovered in both examples. Their infinite remainder norms are nevertheless $1$ and $1/8$, respectively.

title: Repair within the exact plane
setup_tex: In Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$, take $D(x,y,z)=z$ and $C(x,y,z)=y-z$. Starting at $(2,2,3)$, first project to the locally exact plane $z=0$. The two planes encode different constraints on the same raw point.
reading_tex: The local correction reaches $(2,2,0)$. Solving the matching problem inside that plane reaches $(2,0,0)$, with perpendicular squared movements $9$ and $4$. Projecting instead onto the entire plane $y=z$ reaches $(2,1,1)$: matching is repaired, but the local equation has been broken.
experiment_tex: At the unrestricted answer, evaluate both defects: $C(2,1,1)=0$ and $D(2,1,1)=1$. The joint answer has both defects zero and total squared correction $13$.

title: How much can a preservation rule cost?
setup_tex: Keep the raw point $x=(1,0,0)$ and equation $D(x)=x_1$ fixed. Vary the allowed unit correction direction $v=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi)$, with protected observable $p=I-vv^{\mathsf T}$. All three coordinates use the Euclidean metric.
reading_tex: For $0\le\theta<\pi/2$, the unique feasible correction is $a=v/\cos\theta$. Its norm is $\sec\theta$; its endpoint $x-a$ lies in the shaded exact plane. Azimuth changes the answer without changing its cost. At $\theta=\pi/2$, allowed changes cannot alter $x_1$, so this raw point becomes infeasible.
experiment_tex: Compare $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$: the costs are $2/\sqrt3$ and $2$. Turning the correction toward the exact plane increases its length; every plotted line preserves its own declared observable exactly.

title: Small operators can have widely separated kernels
setup_tex: Compare the row operators $D_{s,\theta}=s(\cos\theta\ \ \sin\theta)$ and $D_{s,0}=s(1\ \ 0)$, with $s>0$ and $0\le\theta\le\pi/2$. Their kernels are lines in one Euclidean plane. Sweep both scale and angle; the plot starts at $5^\circ$.
reading_tex: The operator difference is $2s\sin(\theta/2)$, while the projector difference is $\sin\theta$ for the angles shown. Shrinking $s$ changes only the left panel. Each nonzero operator has least residual gain $1/s$: the scale that hides the operator difference also weakens its stability certificate.
experiment_tex: At $\theta=60^\circ$, reducing $s$ from $1$ to $10^{-3}$ reduces the operator difference by a thousand. The projector gap stays $\sqrt3/2$. The zero-scale operator has a different kernel and is excluded.

title: Can one residual history conceal two different outcomes?
setup_tex: Let $u_n^{(p)}=\sum_{k=1}^n k^{-p}$ and $f_n^{(p)}=(s,u_n^{(p)},2^{-n})$. Protect the coordinate $s$, and measure candidate movement with the $\ell^1$ metric. Both paths start at the same point and have the same residual.
reading_tex: The movement through step $N$ is exactly $\sum_{k=1}^N k^{-p}+1-2^{-N}$. For $p=2$ it converges to $1+\pi^2/6$, giving an exact limit. For $p=1$ the unprotected coordinate diverges. These conclusions use the convergent square series and divergent harmonic series, not extrapolation from the finite curves.
experiment_tex: After one step, both paths have residual $1/2$. Nevertheless their eventual behavior differs. The finite residual table alone cannot decide convergence: a summable bound must control movement in the candidate space.

title: Where does a family of data stop being realizable?
setup_tex: Keep $Ta=(a_n/n)$ on $\ell^2$ fixed, and vary the datum $r_n^{(s)}=n^{-s}$ for $s>1/2$. The least correction satisfying its first $N$ equations has energy $E_N(s)=\sum_{n=1}^N n^{2-2s}$.
reading_tex: An exact preimage must have coordinates $a_n=n^{1-s}$. Thus the square-series test gives realizability precisely for $s>3/2$. At $s=3/2$, the energy is harmonic and still diverges. Every finite problem remains solvable on both sides; only a uniform energy bound can pass to the Hilbert realization.
experiment_tex: Predict the middle curve: at $s=3/2$ its energy lies between $\log(N+1)$ and $1+\log N$. Slow growth is still unbounded growth. The plot evaluates finite sums through $N=4096$.

title: When does more correction stop improving the fit?
setup_tex: Let $T(a,b)=(a,b/2,0)$ and $r_h=(1,1,h)$, with Euclidean norms. The correction ball maps to a flat ellipse. Vary its radius $M$ and compare targets at heights $h=0$ and $h=1/2$.
reading_tex: The regularized corrections $a_\alpha=(1/(1+\alpha),2/(1+4\alpha))$ trace the exact frontier at their own budgets. At $M=\sqrt5$, the horizontal mismatch disappears; the residual floor is $|h|$. The shaded band allows data error $\delta=0.03$ and operator error $\eta=0.05$, using width $\delta+\eta M$ on one fixed correction space.
experiment_tex: At the marked point, $\alpha=1$, $a=(1/2,2/5)$ and $M=\sqrt{41}/10$. For $h=1/2$, the residual is $(1/2,4/5,1/2)$; its normalized direction certifies the entire budget ball.

title: Can a better measured fit give a worse answer?
setup_tex: Use $T=\operatorname{diag}(1,0.02)$ and true correction $a^\dagger=(1,0)$. Add the deterministic data error $(0,0.02)$, entirely in the weak mode. The measured datum is $(1,0.02)$; all norms are Euclidean.
reading_tex: The exact regularized answer is $a_\alpha=(1/(1+\alpha),0.0004/(0.0004+\alpha))$. As $\alpha$ decreases, measured fit improves throughout, but the weak-mode error eventually grows. At zero-parameter limit the measured equations are fitted exactly by $(1,1)$, a distance one from the true answer. This is a finite two-mode calculation.
experiment_tex: At $\alpha=0.02$, the answer is $(50/51,1/51)$ and its true error is $\sqrt2/51$. Smaller measured residual alone therefore does not select the most accurate correction for this noisy datum.

title: What happens when basis vectors nearly coincide?
setup_tex: Keep $T=I$, $\alpha=1$, datum $r=(0,-1)$ and proposal $a=0$ fixed in $\mathbb R^2$. Use the full basis $B_e=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&e\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ for $e>0$. Its columns approach the same direction.
reading_tex: The actual normal residual is always $g=(0,1)$, but its coordinate covector is $q=B_e^{\mathsf T}g=(0,e)$. With $G=B_e^{\mathsf T}B_e$, the invariant square is $q^{\mathsf T}G^{-1}q=1$. At $e=0$ the columns no longer span the permitted space, so the full-space certificate formula no longer applies.
experiment_tex: For $e=0.01$, the raw coordinate norm is $0.01$, although the invariant norm is one. The optimizer remains $(0,-1/2)$, and the unchanged proposal still has optimizer error $1/2$.

title: Which stopping schedules preserve convergence?
setup_tex: For the attainable diagonal datum $r_n=1/n^2$, choose $m=\lceil\delta^{-p/2}\rceil$, $\alpha=m^{-2}$, and solver tolerance $\varepsilon=\delta^q$, where $0<\delta\le1$. Vary the positive exponents $p,q$ instead of fixing one noise schedule.
reading_tex: The proved bias, noise and solver bounds have orders $\delta^{p/4}$, $\delta^{1-p/2}$ and $\delta^{q-p}$. All vanish in the colored region $0<p<2$, $q>p$. Its color records their slowest exponent. The uncolored region loses this sufficient guarantee; it does not assert failure of every actual solver.
experiment_tex: The marked choice $(p,q)=(4/3,5/3)$ balances all three exponents at $1/3$. Choosing $q=p$ instead leaves a nonvanishing solver bound. The ceiling is retained in the underlying parameter rule.
